games.explanation: Bryan Woo against right-handed bats has been one of the quieter dominance stories of the year, which is exactly why a plus-money dog price on the Athletics feels lazier than it should. The sim spits out a 3.6 to 3.6 game in a park that suppresses runs harder than almost anywhere in the league, and roof-closed baseball in Seattle is not the environment where you talk yourself into laying juice on a coin flip. Woo's whiff rates dip meaningfully against lefties, which is where McNeil and Butler live, and the Mariners lineup is good but not so good that a one-run game becomes a mismatch. At +175, you're being paid like this is a blowout waiting to happen, and the projected score says it's anything but.

picks.explanation: Nobody wants to touch the Angels against Skenes, which is exactly why the number is fat enough to be interesting. The read here isn't that Los Angeles wins, it's that Skenes games turn into 3-2 grinders where a run and a half is a small ocean, and the sim has this landing inside a run more often than the market thinks. Neto and Trout are the kind of righty bats that Skenes handles best, but he's also a pitcher whose ERA outruns his contact profile, and Pittsburgh's offense isn't the type to blow anyone out on a cool night with the wind blowing in. Getting +1.5 at a shade over even money on a projected two-run game is the whole ballgame.

Cleveland getting laid as a meaningful home favorite requires believing Gavin Williams is the kind of arm that puts games away early, and the walk rate says he is not. He hands out free passes at nearly a 12% clip and the Tigers happen to run out a lineup full of lefties who see him best, with Dingler and Torres both posting numbers north of a .390 xwOBA against right-handed pitching in their platoon splits. Jobe is the shakier starter, nobody's arguing that, but run-line prices are about game shape, and the shape here is a sloppy walk-heavy affair that stays within a run. Getting plus juice on a coin-flip cover against a starter who can't stop issuing traffic is the whole ballgame.

Seattle is a heavy chalk in a game the simulations peg as a dead heat, which is what happens when a market sees "Athletics" and stops reading. The projected score lands at 3.6 apiece under a closed roof in one of the league's stingiest run environments, so the path to Woo throwing a gem and the A's losing by four is narrower than the price suggests. Woo is very good, but he's a fly ball righty in a park that swallows fly balls, and one swing from Butler or a Gelof mistake keeps this inside the number. Getting a run and a half in a projected one-run fight is the entire ballgame.
